### 1. Understanding the Conjugacy Problem in Orthogonal Groups

The classification of elements in the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(V)$ of a non-degenerate quadratic space $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ relies on their Jordan canonical forms (generalized eigenvalues). The conjugacy classes in $\mathrm{O}(V)$ are finer than those in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$. Two matrices $A, B \in \mathrm{O}(V)$ are conjugate in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ if they have the same Jordan structure (same number of blocks of each size for each eigenvalue). They are conjugate in $\mathrm{O}(V)$ if and only if they are conjugate in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ **and** their signatures match in a specific way involving the odd-sized Jordan blocks.

The key insight comes from the theory of orthogonal similarity, often detailed in works by Knapp or in the context of the "twisted" character or signature of the odd part of the Jordan form.
Specifically, for an element $\sigma \in \mathrm{O}(V)$, let its characteristic polynomial be factored into:
- $(x+1)^{m_+}$ and $(x-1)^{m_-}$ (eigenvalues $\pm 1$).
- Irreducible polynomials $p_i(x)$ of odd degree (Type I? or Type O? The prompt distinguishes Type O and Type I later).
- Reciprocal pairs $q_j(x)q_j^*(x)$ (Type II? or Type O/I? The prompt mentions Type O and Type I factors).

Two isometries $\sigma, \tau$ conjugate in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ are conjugate in $\mathrm{O}(V)$ if and only if the signature of the subspace $V_{\sigma}^{\mathrm{odd}}$ equals the signature of $V_{\tau}^{\mathrm{odd}}$.
